title: Uniqueness of the center of complete mixability
statement: For a distribution F on R (or R^d), can F be n-completely mixable with two different centers? Equivalently, writing M_n(mu) for the set of distributions that are n-CM with center mu, is M_n(mu) intersect M_n(nu) empty for all mu != nu?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 'complete mixability joint mixability open problems Wang 2014 solved uniform convex set n-CM' surfaced Puccetti, Rigo, B. Wang and R. Wang, 'Centers of probability measures without the mean', arXiv:1704.02660, J. Theoret. Probab. 32 (2019). Abstract read: for each n >= 2 there exist n standard Cauchy variables summing to a constant C if and only if |C| <= n log(n-1)/pi, so the center is NOT unique; uniqueness holds when at least n-2 of the n margins have a finite mean. This answers Open Problem 1 in the negative.
resolved_by: Puccetti, Rigo, B. Wang and R. Wang, 'Centers of probability measures without the mean', arXiv:1704.02660, J. Theoret. Probab. 32 (2019) 1482-1501. Centers form a nondegenerate interval for the standard Cauchy law; uniqueness holds as soon as n-2 margins are integrable. Abstract read on 2026-09-08; full text not fetched (bounded recall).

title: A generic (probabilistic or analytic) proof of the main complete/joint mixability theorems
statement: All known sufficient conditions for n-complete mixability (symmetric unimodal density; monotone density with the mean condition a+(b-a)/n <= mu <= b-(b-a)/n; concave density; density bounded below by 3/(n(b-a)); Gaussian and elliptical families) are proved case by case, by discretisation plus combinatorial rearrangement. Is there a single generic probabilistic or analytic proof that yields them together, for instance through the duality of Theorem 1 of the source?
status_search: Same WebSearch as D0001, plus a reading of Sections 2.2-2.3 of the source. The follow-up literature located (Wang and Wang, 'Joint Mixability', Math. Oper. Res.; Puccetti and Wang 2015; the elliptical-family paper arXiv:1706.05499) still proves each class by discretisation into n-discrete uniform distributions; no unified proof appeared in the searched results. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Look for one construction that reproduces several of the listed theorems at once. Candidate mechanism: an orbit (odometer) construction. Write F as the law of g(U), U uniform on [0,1]. If there is a measure-preserving map T of [0,1] with T^n = identity such that sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k u) = n*mu for a.e. u, then (g(U), g(TU), ..., g(T^{n-1}U)) is a complete mix, so F is n-CM.
attempt.result: The orbit criterion is genuinely generic and immediately covers two of the listed families. (i) F symmetric about mu, n=2: take T(u)=1-u; then g(u)+g(1-u)=2mu by symmetry, so every symmetric law is 2-CM, and with the concatenation rule (n-CM and m-CM imply (n+m)-CM) this recovers 'symmetric unimodal is n-CM' for all even n. (ii) In R^d the same criterion with T induced by a linear map of finite order proves a whole class at once: if C is an affine image of a body invariant under a linear R with R^n = I and no nonzero fixed vector, then Unif(C) is n-CM, because sum_{k<n} R^k = 0. This yields simplices and ellipsoids simultaneously (see D0005) and is not in the source.
attempt.obstruction: The sharp monotone-density theorem is not of orbit type. Its extremal complete mixes are built by an n-dependent greedy rearrangement of the quantile function and the coupling is not generated by any finite group action: when mu sits at an endpoint of the admissible interval the complete mix is rigid (see D0010) and non-exchangeable, so no T with T^n = id can produce it. A generic proof therefore has to leave the group-orbit world and produce a measurable selection from the feasibility problem of Theorem 1, and that is where the argument stalls: the dual certificate of Theorem 1(iii) is a pure existence statement with no known normal form.
attempt.key_identity: sum_{k=0}^{n-1} R^k = 0 whenever R^n = I and 1 is not an eigenvalue of R.

title: Is the binary-multinomial layer decomposition (Theorem 3) useful for characterising CM/JM classes?
statement: Theorem 3 of the source states that a Z_+^n-valued vector X is a joint mix with integer center N if and only if X = sum_{k=1}^N X_k where each X_k is a binary multinomial vector (values in {0,1}^n with exactly one coordinate equal to 1). Can this decomposition, which is 'perpendicular' to the n-discrete-uniform decomposition of Theorem 2, be used in a non-trivial way to characterise further classes of completely or jointly mixable distributions?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the survey's follow-up literature ('joint mixability Wang Wang', 'complete mixability open questions'); every paper located (Wang and Wang Math. Oper. Res.; Puccetti and Wang 2015; arXiv:1706.05499) uses the Theorem-2 style decomposition into n-discrete uniforms, none uses the layer decomposition. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Read Theorem 3 as an allocation statement: a Z_+-valued joint mix with center N is exactly a way of throwing N labelled balls into n boxes (one ball per layer), with box i receiving F_i-many balls. Then ask what stacking independent layer systems gives.
attempt.result: Two non-trivial consequences follow immediately, so the answer to the source's question is yes. (a) Layer concatenation: if (F_1,...,F_n) is JM with integer center N and (G_1,...,G_n) is JM with integer center M, then stacking the two independent layer stacks shows (F_1*G_1,...,F_n*G_n) is JM with center N+M -- a convolution stability that is invisible in the Theorem-2 picture. (b) A new explicit family: for any p_1,...,p_n >= 0 with sum p_i = 1 and any N in N, the tuple (Bin(N,p_1),...,Bin(N,p_n)) is JM with joint center N; take N i.i.d. layers, each placing its single 1 in coordinate i with probability p_i. Setting all p_i = 1/n recovers the source's own remark that Bin(n,1/n) is n-CM, which is therefore the diagonal case of a two-parameter family.
attempt.obstruction: The construction is confined to integer centers and Z_+-valued margins, and it produces layers that are exchangeable in k. The interesting theorems (monotone density, concave density) survive discretisation only as laws on a fine lattice, and the corresponding complete mixes are NOT layer-i.i.d.; forcing a layer decomposition there gives layers with a dependence structure the theorem does not constrain, so no new sufficient condition on F alone is obtained. The missing ingredient is a criterion, in terms of the margins only, for the existence of a layer stack with prescribed marginal counts -- which is again the feasibility problem of D0012.
attempt.key_identity: X is a joint mix with center N iff X = sum_{k=1}^N X_k with each X_k binary multinomial; independent stacks convolve the margins and add the centers.

title: Is the law-determined-norm inequality sufficient for complete mixability?
statement: Theorem 5 of the source shows that if F with mean mu is n-CM then ||(X-t)_+|| <= (n-1)||(X-s)_-|| and ||(X-t)_-|| <= (n-1)||(X-s)_+|| for every law-determined (rearrangement-invariant, possibly infinite-valued) norm ||.||, every t in R and s = (n*mu - t)/(n-1). Suppose these inequalities hold for all law-determined norms and all t. Under what extra conditions is this sufficient for F to be n-CM? A subsidiary question raised in the same paragraph is to characterise all law-determined norms in the sense of Definition 5.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0002; no paper found proving a converse to Theorem 5. The two special cases named in the source (the L-infinity norm giving the mean condition (15), the L2 norm giving the Gaussian JM criterion 2 max sigma_i <= sum sigma_i) remain the only instances where the necessary condition is known to be sufficient. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Test the strength of the family of inequalities by evaluating it on the norms it can see. The family is indexed by rearrangement-invariant functionals and each inequality involves only the one-dimensional laws of (X-t)_+ and (X-s)_-.
attempt.result: For n=2 the answer is YES with no extra condition, and the proof is short: s = 2mu - t, and the two inequalities read ||(X-t)_+|| <= ||(X-(2mu-t))_-|| and ||(X-t)_-|| <= ||(X-(2mu-t))_+||. Since (X-(2mu-t))_- = ((2mu-t)-X)_+ and rearrangement-invariant functionals separate laws of nonnegative variables (the family ||Y||_p, p in [1,infinity], already determines the law of Y >= 0 through its moments when Y is bounded, and through the family E[(Y-c)_+] in general), running t over R forces (X-t)_+ and ((2mu-t)-X)_+ to be equidistributed for every t, i.e. F is symmetric about mu, which is exactly 2-CM. For n >= 3 the same computation gives only one-sided tail comparisons with the factor (n-1) and cannot force symmetry: the family sees F only through the pair of truncated half-laws, and n-CM for n >= 3 is not a function of that pair.
attempt.obstruction: A counterexample for n = 3 must be a law satisfying every truncated-tail comparison but failing 3-CM; the natural candidates are unimodal laws with the mean condition (15) tight. I could not construct one, because verifying (14) for EVERY law-determined norm requires knowing the class of such norms, and that is precisely the subsidiary question the source leaves open. This is the exact wall: without a Kusuoka-type representation for possibly infinite-valued rearrangement-invariant functionals, the hypothesis cannot be checked on any concrete candidate.
attempt.key_identity: n = 2: the hypothesis for all t and all rearrangement-invariant norms is equivalent to symmetry of F about mu, which is equivalent to 2-CM.

title: Is the uniform distribution on a convex body in R^d completely mixable of order d+1?
statement: Let C be a convex set in R^d. Is the uniform distribution on C necessarily n-CM for every n >= d+1? The source states the problem is equivalent to (d+1)-complete mixability and records only the trivial cases d=0 and d=1.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 'complete mixability joint mixability uniform convex set n-CM' returned the source itself plus the follow-up literature (Wang and Wang Math. Oper. Res.; Puccetti and Wang 2015; the elliptical-distribution paper arXiv:1706.05499, which settles ellipsoids in a wider setting). No result covering a general convex body was found. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Use the orbit construction of D0002 in R^d. If R is a linear map with R^n = I and 1 not an eigenvalue of R, and C is invariant under R about its centroid, then (X, RX, ..., R^{n-1}X) with X uniform on C is a complete mix, since sum_{k<n} R^k = 0. Then push forward by affine maps, under which uniformity and complete mixability are both preserved.
attempt.result: This settles the problem for two natural families in every dimension. (i) EVERY simplex in R^d is (d+1)-CM. For the regular simplex the rotation R cyclically permuting the d+1 vertices acts on the d-dimensional span of the centred vertices as the standard representation of Z_{d+1}, which contains no invariant vector, hence sum_{k=0}^{d} R^k = 0 and (X, RX, ..., R^d X) is a (d+1)-complete mix; every simplex is an affine image T(x) = Ax + b of the regular one, and sum_k T(R^k X) = A*0 + (d+1)b is constant. (ii) Every ellipsoid is n-CM for every n >= 2 (rotate by 2pi/n in a plane, or use central symmetry). (iii) More generally, every affine image of a body admitting a fixed-point-free linear symmetry of order n is n-CM. Separately I record a gap in the source's own framing: the claim that the problem is EQUIVALENT to (d+1)-CM is not obvious for bodies without central symmetry, because the usual route from (d+1)-CM to all n >= d+1 uses concatenation with 2-CM, and 2-CM of Unif(C) is exactly central symmetry of C about its centroid, which a scalene triangle does not have. So for a scalene triangle the case n = 4 of Open Problem 5 is not implied by the case n = 3 that I prove here.
attempt.obstruction: A generic convex body has a trivial affine automorphism group, so the orbit route gives nothing there. What is needed is a (d+1)-complete mix built from convexity alone. The natural attempt -- decompose C into simplices and mix each piece -- fails because the pieces have DIFFERENT centroids, so their (d+1)-mixes have different centers and the mixture over pieces is not a complete mix (mixing complete mixes requires a common center, see D0007). Making the centers agree is a transport constraint that convexity does not obviously supply.
attempt.key_identity: sum_{k=0}^{n-1} R^k = 0 for fixed-point-free R of order n; affine images of complete mixes are complete mixes.

title: Does complete mixability of all lower-dimensional projections imply complete mixability in R^d?
statement: Let F be a distribution on R^d, d > 1, such that the projection of F onto every essential subspace of R^d is n-CM. With what extra conditions is this sufficient for F to be n-CM on R^d? (Proposition 6 of the source gives the converse direction.)
status_search: Searched 2026-09-08 together with D0005. The only multi-dimensional mixability results found (arXiv:1706.05499 for elliptical families and Section 2.5 of the source) are sufficient conditions of a different type; nothing asserting or refuting a projective criterion. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Ask whether the coupling can be assembled direction by direction. Projection onto a line L gives a complete mix of the projected law; a positive answer needs these one-dimensional mixes, for a spanning family of lines, to be the projections of a single R^d-valued coupling.
attempt.result: The problem is exactly a projective consistency (Kolmogorov-type) question, and that reformulation is the content of this attempt: since X_1 + ... + X_n = n*mu in R^d if and only if <u, X_1 + ... + X_n> = n<u,mu> for every u in the unit sphere, F is n-CM if and only if there exists a SINGLE coupling all of whose scalar projections are complete mixes. So the hypothesis of the problem (each projection is separately n-CM) is the projective family of solutions, and the missing step is a selection that is consistent across directions. I also checked the obvious would-be separating example: Unif on a scalene triangle in R^2 has every one-dimensional projection with a concave density, hence 3-CM by item (c) of the source, and the body itself is 3-CM by D0005, so it does not separate; and for n = 2 both the hypothesis and the conclusion fail (projections are unimodal but not symmetric), so it does not separate either.
attempt.obstruction: The consistency question is infinite-dimensional: the one-dimensional complete mix in a given direction is massively non-unique, and there is no known selection principle picking a projectively consistent branch. Extra conditions that would obviously work (rotational invariance of F; uniqueness of the complete mix in every direction) are strong enough to give the result directly by symmetry, so they do not answer the question in the spirit intended. That is the wall.
attempt.key_identity: X_1 + ... + X_n = n*mu in R^d iff <u, sum X_i> = n<u,mu> for all u in S^{d-1}.

title: Is every absolutely continuous law on a bounded interval n-completely mixable for all large n?
statement: Puccetti, Wang and Wang show that a law on [a,b] with density f(x) >= 3/(n(b-a)) is n-CM, so any absolutely continuous law with a density bounded away from zero is n-CM for all large n. Can the lower bound on the density be dropped: is every absolutely continuous distribution on a bounded interval n-CM for all sufficiently large n?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as above; the surveys located (Puccetti and Wang 2015; Wang and Wang Math. Oper. Res.) still cite the density lower bound of Puccetti, Wang and Wang as the state of the art, and none of the results found removes it. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Try to reduce to the known theorem by splitting F. Write F as a mixture of pieces each of which is n-CM, and try to align the centers.
attempt.result: Two positive observations and a sharp obstruction. (1) Mixing preserves complete mixability WITH A COMMON CENTER: if F_1 and F_2 are both n-CM with the same center mu then any mixture of them is n-CM with center mu (mix the couplings). Since the center of an integrable n-CM law is forced to be its mean, a decomposition F = sum_j w_j F_j works precisely when the pieces can be chosen with a common mean equal to mean(F). (2) Consequently the answer is YES for every absolutely continuous F that admits a measure-preserving involution of [a,b] pushing F to its reflection about its mean (pair pieces symmetrically about the mean and use 2-CM on each pair, then concatenate) -- this reproves the symmetric case and extends it to laws that are only 'pairable' rather than symmetric.
attempt.obstruction: For a generic absolutely continuous F the pieces cannot be paired to a common mean because the density may vanish on a set that is asymmetric about the mean: e.g. a density supported on [0,1] union [10,11] with unequal masses has only two candidate conditional means and no pairing of pieces about the global mean. One is then forced to use genuine n-fold combinations, i.e. to control the joint law of the number of items falling in each component of the support while keeping the sum exactly constant. No known argument produces exact a.s. equality with a positive probability for every admissible count vector; all known proofs build the mix by a greedy water-filling of the quantile function, which needs the density lower bound to guarantee the filling never gets stuck. That is the precise wall.
attempt.key_identity: Mixing complete mixes with a common center gives a complete mix; the center of an integrable n-CM law is its mean.

title: An explicit copula for a complete mix
statement: Suppose F satisfies one of the known sufficient conditions (for instance a monotone density with the mean condition) and hence is n-CM. Write down an explicit copula of an n-complete mix with margins F, equivalently of a joint mix with given margins.
status_search: Searched 2026-09-08 with D0009. The rearrangement-algorithm literature (Embrechts, Puccetti and Rueschendorf) produces numerical couplings rather than closed-form copulas, and no closed form for the monotone-density case appeared in the results. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Compute the copula in the two cases where the complete mix is explicit: symmetric F with n=2, and the orbit construction of D0002.
attempt.result: In both explicit cases the copula is singular and carried by a one-dimensional set, which explains the absence of a closed form in general and tells one where to look. For n=2 and F symmetric about mu the unique complete mix is (X, 2mu - X), whose copula is the countermonotonic copula W(u,v) = max(u+v-1, 0). For an orbit construction driven by a measure-preserving n-cycle T of [0,1] the copula is a shuffle of Min carried by the graph of T; when T is the rotation u -> u + 1/n mod 1 (the complete mix of Unif[0,1] after a monotone change of variables) the copula is concentrated on the n parallel diagonal segments v_k = u + k/n mod 1. So the correct ansatz for the monotone-density class is a shuffle-of-Min type copula, which reduces the search from all copulas to measure-preserving n-cycles of [0,1].
attempt.obstruction: The sharp monotone-density complete mix is NOT of shuffle-of-Min type when the mean lies strictly inside the admissible interval: there the mix splits the support into a part contributing n-1 items and a part contributing one item, with a realisation-dependent split point, so the coupling is not a deterministic permutation of a single quantile variable. Writing it down amounts to solving a free-boundary problem for the quantile function, which is exactly what the combinatorial proof of the theorem avoids doing. That is the wall.
attempt.key_identity: n=2 symmetric case: C = W; orbit case: C is the shuffle of Min induced by the n-cycle T.

title: Exact simulation of a complete mix
statement: Suppose F satisfies one of the known sufficient conditions and hence is n-CM. Give an algorithm that samples exactly from an n-complete mix with margins F.
status_search: Searched 2026-09-08 with D0008. The rearrangement algorithm of Embrechts, Puccetti and Rueschendorf and the swapping algorithms cited in Section 2.11 of the source are approximate, and the source itself says their convergence conditions are unclear. No exact sampler found. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Use the representation theorem (Theorem 2 of the source): F is n-CM with center mu if and only if F = integral F_a dh(a) with F_a the n-discrete uniform law on a, over the hyperplane {a in R^n : a.1 = n*mu}. An exact sampler is then 'sample a from h; output a uniformly random coordinate of a'.
attempt.result: This turns exact simulation into the problem of sampling from the mixing measure h on the hyperplane, a reformulation the source does not state. For the explicit families the sampler is immediate: for symmetric F and n=2, h is the law of (X, 2mu - X); for an orbit construction h is the law of (g(U), g(TU), ..., g(T^{n-1}U)). For the monotone-density class one obtains an exact sampler for the DISCRETISED law by running the source's discretisation to N atoms and using the finite decomposition into n-discrete uniforms, with total variation error to F equal to the discretisation error, which is O(1/N) for a Lipschitz quantile function.
attempt.obstruction: Exactness is lost precisely at the discretisation step and cannot be repaired: the target constraint is an a.s. equality, so an approximate sample has sum n*mu + O(1/N) and no rejection, coupling-from-the-past or refinement scheme can move it to exactly n*mu while keeping the margins exactly F. An exact sampler therefore requires h itself, which is the same free-boundary object as in D0008. That is the wall.
attempt.key_identity: F is n-CM with center mu iff F = integral over {a.1 = n mu} of F_a dh(a) with F_a the n-discrete uniform law on a.

title: Extra conditions making a unimodal law on a bounded interval completely mixable
statement: Counterexamples are known showing that the mean condition a + (b-a)/n <= mu <= b - (b-a)/n is not sufficient for the complete mixability of a law with a unimodal density on a bounded interval. Under what extra conditions is a unimodal distribution on a bounded interval n-CM? The case of interest is when one of the inequalities in the mean condition is an equality.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for D0002. The sufficient conditions found in the follow-up literature remain monotone density (sharp), concave density, symmetric unimodal density, and the density lower bound; nothing giving a criterion for general unimodal densities. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Examine the boundary case mu = a + (b-a)/n, where the mean condition is tight, and read off what a complete mix must look like there.
attempt.result: At the boundary the complete mix is rigid, and this yields a necessary condition not stated in the source. If mu = a + (b-a)/n and F is n-CM with center mu, then for the complete mix sum_i (X_i - a) = n*mu - n*a = b - a, while 0 <= X_i - a <= b - a for every i. So (X_i - a)_{i<=n} is an exchangeable random composition of the FIXED total b - a into n nonnegative parts, with common marginal law F(. + a). Applying the elementary bound P(max_i (X_i - a) > x) <= (b-a)/x valid for any composition of total b-a (at most (b-a)/x parts can exceed x), and exchangeability, gives n*(1 - F(a + x)) <= (b-a)/x, i.e. F(a+x) >= 1 - (b-a)/(n x) for every x in (0, b-a]. Any unimodal density on [a,b] whose mean is at the left boundary of the mean condition and which is too flat near a violates this and is therefore NOT n-CM. This gives a clean quantitative extra necessary condition in the tight case, which is the case the source singles out.
attempt.obstruction: Away from the boundary the composition structure disappears, and the necessary condition above degrades to the mean condition itself. Converting it into a sufficient condition requires an existence theorem for exchangeable random compositions with a prescribed one-dimensional marginal, which is the same feasibility problem as in D0007 and D0012. That is the wall.
attempt.key_identity: At mu = a + (b-a)/n a complete mix is an exchangeable random composition of b-a into n nonnegative parts, forcing F(a+x) >= 1 - (b-a)/(n x).

title: When does the aggregation set contain a convex-order smallest element?
statement: Let D_n = {X_1 + ... + X_n : X_i ~ F_i} be the aggregation set of a Frechet class. A counterexample is known in which D_n has no smallest element in convex order, yet for all commonly used margins such an element exists. What are necessary and sufficient conditions on (F_1,...,F_n) for D_n to contain a smallest element with respect to convex order?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 'convolution bounds on quantile aggregation' surfaced arXiv:2007.09320 (Blanchet, Lam, Liu, Wang), which from its abstract computes sharp convolution bounds rather than characterising attainment of a convex-order minimum. No paper found stating necessary and sufficient conditions for attainment. No evidence of resolution.

attempt.method: Separate the two issues: existence of a convex-order lower bound for D_n, and its attainment inside D_n. Use the fact that convex order is generated by the family phi_t(x) = (x-t)_+.
attempt.result: The problem is exactly a simultaneity problem, which is the content of this attempt. D_n is convex, tight (the margins are fixed) and closed in the weak topology, so for each fixed t the infimum of E[(S-t)_+] over S in D_n is ATTAINED by a compactness argument. Hence D_n contains a convex-order smallest element if and only if a single coupling attains the infimum for every t simultaneously. If (F_1,...,F_n) is jointly mixable the constant is that element and attainment is trivial; the known counterexample must therefore be a case where the t-indexed optimisers genuinely move with t.
attempt.obstruction: Characterising when the optimisers do not move is the wall. For fixed t the minimiser of E[(S-t)_+] has the standard structure behind the rearrangement algorithm -- a comonotonic piece on the tails and a 'mixing' piece in the middle, with the split determined by t -- and I have no characterisation of the margins for which this split is independent of t, beyond the jointly mixable case and the case n=2 with one degenerate margin.
attempt.key_identity: X <=_cx Y iff E[(X-t)_+] <= E[(Y-t)_+] for all t; a smallest element exists iff one coupling minimises all these functionals at once.

title: Characterising the aggregation set of a Frechet class
statement: Characterise D_n = {X_1 + ... + X_n : X_i ~ F_i}: for a given distribution G, decide whether some S ~ G lies in D_n. The only fully characterised case is n=2 with Bernoulli margins; the problem is open for all n >= 2 in general. In the i.i.d. case D_n* = {S/n : S in D_n} has upper limit C_F = {S : S <=_cx X, X ~ F} as n -> infinity, but D_n* is strictly contained in C_F for finite n.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Closest hits were arXiv:2007.09320 'Convolution bounds on quantile aggregation' and arXiv:1811.11981 'Sums of standard uniform random variables'; the latter characterises which laws arise as sums of standard uniforms, i.e. one special case of D_n. I did not fetch it and therefore cannot certify how much of D_n it determines. Recorded as open with a flagged partial-resolution lead for the uniform-margin case.

attempt.method: Identify the exact structure of D_n as a convex set and locate the source of the difficulty via the same duality that gives Theorem 1 of the source.
attempt.result: D_n is convex (mix the couplings), tight, weakly closed, and contains the independent and the comonotonic sums. By the duality of Theorem 1(iii), G is NOT in D_n if and only if there exist measurable f_1,...,f_n and g with sum_i f_i(x_i) >= g(x_1 + ... + x_n) pointwise but sum_i integral f_i dF_i < integral g dG. So membership in D_n is a separation problem, and the difficulty is entirely in the absence of a normal form for the dual certificate (f_1,...,f_n,g).
attempt.obstruction: For n=2 with Bernoulli margins the dual certificate lives in a finite-dimensional space and can be enumerated, which is exactly why that case is solved. For continuous margins the dual is an infinite family of one-dimensional functions whose extreme rays are not classified. In addition the source itself records that deciding joint mixability of discrete uniform laws on Z is NP-complete, which is strong evidence that no tractable characterisation exists even in the discrete case; the honest reformulation is to ask for a description of the convex-order CLOSURE of D_n, where the n -> infinity limit C_F is already known.
attempt.key_identity: G not in D_n iff there are f_i and g with sum_i f_i(x_i) >= g(sum_i x_i) pointwise and sum_i int f_i dF_i < int g dG.
